content: Nabumetone is metabolized in the liver to produce 6-methoxy-2-naphthylacetic acid (6MNA), its active metabolite, while approximately 50% of the drug is converted into unidentified metabolites that are subsequently excreted in the urine. After oral administration of nabumetone tablets, 6MNA demonstrates pharmacokinetic properties consistent with a one-compartment model, characterized by first-order absorption and elimination kinetics. More than 99% of 6MNA is bound to plasma proteins. The unbound fraction of 6MNA is influenced by its total plasma concentration and is dose-proportional within the range of 1000 mg to 2000 mg. At steady state, following daily administration of 2000 mg, approximately 8% of the total plasma concentration is unbound. Steady-state plasma concentrations of 6MNA are slightly lower than those predicted from single-dose data. This discrepancy is likely due to the increased hepatic clearance of the unbound fraction of 6MNA. Co-administration of food enhances the rate of absorption and the subsequent appearance of 6MNA in plasma but does not alter the extent of conversion of nabumetone to 6MNA. Peak plasma concentrations of 6MNA increase by approximately one-third when nabumetone is taken with food. Co-administration with an aluminum-containing antacid does not significantly affect the bioavailability of 6MNA. Simulated pharmacokinetic curves indicate the range of active metabolite plasma concentrations expected in 95% of patients receiving 1000 mg to 2000 mg doses of nabumetone at steady state. The cross-hatched area in the graph represents the expected interpatient variability in plasma concentrations following oral administration of these doses. 6MNA undergoes hepatic biotransformation to inactive metabolites, which are eliminated as both free metabolites and conjugates. None of the known metabolites of 6MNA have been detected in plasma. Preliminary in vivo and in vitro studies suggest that, unlike other NSAIDs, there is no evidence of enterohepatic recirculation of the active metabolite. Approximately 75% of a radiolabeled dose of nabumetone is recovered in the urine within 48 hours, and about 80% is recovered within 168 hours. An additional 9% of the dose is excreted in the feces. Following oral administration of 1000 mg to 2000 mg doses to steady state, the mean plasma clearance of 6MNA is 20 to 30 mL/min, and its elimination half-life is approximately 24 hours. In elderly patients, steady-state plasma concentrations of 6MNA are generally higher than those observed in younger, healthy subjects. Additionally, there is a 50% increase in the plasma levels of unbound 6MNA in elderly individuals. In patients with moderate renal impairment, renal excretion of 6MNA decreases by an average of 33% compared to normal patients. A similar increase in the mean terminal half-life of 6MNA has been observed in patients with severe renal dysfunction (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min). In patients undergoing hemodialysis, steady-state plasma concentrations of 6MNA are comparable to those in healthy subjects. Due to its extensive protein binding, 6MNA is not dialyzable. Dosage adjustment of nabumetone is generally not necessary in patients with mild renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance ≥50 mL/min). However, caution is advised when prescribing nabumetone to patients with moderate or severe renal insufficiency. The maximum starting doses for patients with moderate or severe renal insufficiency should not exceed 750 mg or 500 mg, respectively, once daily. After careful monitoring of renal function, daily doses may be increased to a maximum of 1500 mg and 1000 mg, respectively. Data on the use of nabumetone in patients with severe hepatic impairment are limited. The biotransformation of nabumetone to 6MNA and the subsequent metabolism of 6MNA to inactive metabolites depend on hepatic function and may be reduced in patients with severe hepatic impairment, such as those with a history of or biopsy-proven cirrhosis. In gastrointestinal studies, nabumetone was compared to aspirin in terms of inducing gastrointestinal blood loss. Studies using 51Cr-tagged red blood cells in healthy males showed no significant difference in fecal blood loss after 3 or 4 weeks of daily administration of nabumetone (1000 mg or 2000 mg) compared to placebo-treated or untreated subjects. In contrast, aspirin (3600 mg daily) caused an increase in fecal blood loss compared to nabumetone-treated, placebo-treated, or untreated subjects. The clinical relevance of these findings is unknown. Endoscopy trials involving patients previously treated with NSAIDs showed varying baseline scores and treatment courses. These trials were not designed to correlate symptoms with endoscopy scores or serious gastrointestinal events. In five clinical trials comparing nabumetone (1000 mg daily) to naproxen (250 mg or 500 mg twice daily) over 3 to 12 weeks, fewer patients treated with nabumetone had endoscopically detected lesions (>3 mm). In two trials comparing nabumetone (1000 mg or 2000 mg daily) to piroxicam (10 mg to 20 mg daily) over 7 to 10 days, fewer nabumetone-treated patients had endoscopically detected lesions. In three trials comparing nabumetone (1000 mg daily) to indomethacin (100 mg to 150 mg daily) over 3 to 4 weeks, endoscopy scores were higher with indomethacin. In a 12-week trial involving 171 patients, nabumetone (1000 mg/day) was compared to ibuprofen (2400 mg/day) and ibuprofen (2400 mg/day) plus misoprostol (800 mcg/day). Patients treated with nabumetone had fewer endoscopically detected lesions (>5 mm) than those treated with ibuprofen alone, but results were comparable to the combination of ibuprofen and misoprostol. These findings did not correlate with abdominal pain. In one-week, repeat-dose studies in healthy volunteers, nabumetone (1000 mg daily) had minimal effects on collagen-induced platelet aggregation and no effect on bleeding time.
